chapter_theme: The brothers of Accuvakkiriivan appear and scorn the human host, the two armies meet in a crowded battle of chariots, elephants and horses, and the warriors fight by a code of fearlessness and mercy.

cast.role: the kings who rose against Ratanupura and fled
an unnamed man who reports the temper of the discus-armed ones
the dark-bodied hero, likely the camper and the sapphire-hued one
the fierce lord of the Vidyadharas whose brothers fight
his younger brothers who lead the sky army
the eldest of the younger brothers
one of the brothers, who laughs at the human host
one of the brothers with curved teeth
one of the brothers who claps and laughs
the fighting men of the two armies

1256.reading: Kings who rose against Ratanupura fought, were ruined and turned their backs in flight; the poet closes that none finishes what he has in mind unless it ripens with difficulty.
1256.nuance: The verse names no cause for the failure, neither fate nor misjudged strength, and gives only the general rule that an aim is won hard.
1256.event: The kings who marched on Ratanupura are broken and flee the field.

claims.claim: a purpose is fulfilled only when it ripens with difficulty; none completes what he intends by wishing

1257.reading: When the enemy's stronghold battle is broken that day, one man reports the temper of the discus-armed ones, and it is like pouring ghee on the fire of the world's end.
1257.nuance: The words at line 3 are run together, so who is reporting, and of whom, is held loosely.
1257.event: One man tells of the temper of the discus-handed ones after the enemy's defeat.

1258.reading: The news of those who went to the sky fainting and of the foes who went to the earth being cut down lodges in the mind like a spear thrust into a wound.
1258.nuance: The subject whose mind is pierced is not named in the verse, so the sense is held loosely.

1259.reading: A broad-minded dark-bodied one, saying that the other should rest and then rise against him, goes and pitches camp with his forces on the hill called Arungalam.
1259.nuance: The verse never names the camper; his dark cloud-like body suggests Tivittan, but this rests on the story so far, not on the verse.
1259.event: The dark-bodied commander encamps his army on the hill Arungalam.

1260.reading: Younger brothers of Accuvakkiriivan, skilled in handling dark rutting elephants, spread a sea of troops across the sky and appear, smiling and breathing venom.
1260.event: Accuvakkiriivan's younger brothers appear in the sky with a spread-out army.

1261.reading: The eldest of the young brothers says that unless they destroy, with their kin, those who wronged their lord, they would sit with bangles and their hair tied.
1261.nuance: Bangles and tied hair mark a woman's state, so the vow stakes manhood on revenge.
1261.event: The eldest of Accuvakkiriivan's brothers vows to kill those who wronged their lord, with all their kin.

claims.claim: a retainer who fails to avenge harm done to his lord forfeits the name of a man

1262.reading: Nilamanikantan, seeing the men with their umbrella-marks, laughs, with his bright tusk-white teeth showing, at these humans who dare to fight against them.
1262.nuance: The first line is hard (மாலுமாங் குடையர்கொன்); the sense of the sneer is held loosely.
1262.event: Nilamanikantan laughs with contempt at the human army.

1263.reading: Vayirakandan, with curved teeth, says the foe will lie rolling on the battlefield, as the mud of garlands wet with honey and the breasts of women are kept for them.
1263.event: Vayirakandan boasts that the enemies will lie rolling on the field.

1264.reading: Sukandan claps hands together and laughs, as snakes would show hatred to Garuda.
1264.nuance: The simile treats the Vidyadharas as serpents mocking the eagle Garuda, an image of overconfidence.
1264.event: Sukandan laughs and claps his hands in scorn.

1265.reading: The fierce one, his cruel heart cooled by his brothers' words, which fall like rain, looks at them and bids them set their names firm upon the earth where those who hated his name are loved.
1265.nuance: The fierce one is probably Accuvakkiriivan speaking to his brothers, but the verse leaves him unnamed.
1265.event: The fierce lord, cooled by his brothers' words, sends them to make their names stand.

claims.claim: a warrior's name is made to stand by victory over those who hate it

1266.reading: As the Vidyadharas press on, their rage swelling like poison burning poison, the sapphire-bright one's army rises without any fraud and stands against them.
1266.event: The Vidyadharas attack and the sapphire-hued commander's army rises and meets them.

1267.reading: The poet says it is not easy for us to count the spear-army that came as far as the sky and the sword-army that met it on the ground, two seas of troops.
1267.nuance: The poet speaks in the first person plural of the effort of counting.

1268.reading: If two seas existed and the land between them were a woman, the two forces would equal them, since the two unconquerable armies match each other.

1269.reading: To one who looks, the host seems to be nothing but crowded strong chariots, nothing but gathered war elephants and nothing but packed horses, all mingled together.

1270.reading: The warriors with right-handed weapons, anklets and sashes, red garlands and red eyes appear as if this world had no room for them and they ruled another.
1270.nuance: The praise makes the warriors too great for this world, which sets the Vidyadharas' scorn in 1262 to 1264 against the foe's real stature.

1271.reading: The armies joined battle; with no direction left for the fighting to spread, the troops stood in a war that was like the world's end.
1271.event: The two armies join in a battle so dense it has no direction to spread.

1272.reading: Some, with drums and flags and garlands struck back and forth, fight one another in their chariots, and their arrows fall thicker than rain from clouds.
1272.event: Warriors in chariots strike drums and garlands and loose showers of arrows on each other.

1273.reading: Feet are packed with feet, shoulders with shoulders, swords with swords; the poet asks in what days these could be counted.
1273.nuance: The closing question asks whether the crush can be counted in any number of days.

1274.reading: Umbrellas hide the ground, flags cover it, the earth is smeared dark, and weapons and the jewels of serpents flash across it.

1275.reading: Elephants strike with their trunks and throw fire between their eyes; as their tusks meet, the great ones seem mountains fighting mountains.

1276.reading: Horses circle like the wheels of time over the helmets of the fierce kings and the heads of rutting elephants.
1276.nuance: The wheel of time (கால சக்கரம்) is a simile only; the verse makes no doctrinal claim.

1277.reading: The bright-bossed shields, the shafts of the quivers and the bow-armed chariot throngs resemble clouds raining arrows.

1278.reading: The kings, with their minds failing to know who would do what and where, act in confusion with gleaming spears and crowded swords.
1278.event: The kings fight in confusion, unsure what to do.

1279.reading: The warriors, with sashes and dark anklets, glare and move about, not fearing even Death, calling that the fearful may leave and those who can bear it stay, and the leaders of unblemished lines go.
1279.event: The warriors call on the fearful to leave the field while the brave stay and fight.

claims.claim: one who fears may withdraw, and only one who does not fear even Death should stay in battle

1280.reading: The victors do not strike scornfully at an enemy who blinks, nor stare shamefully at one who fled, as though showing the foe the heroic path.
1280.nuance: Kural 775 counts a blink at a flung spear as flight; this verse shows the winners declining to press the blinker.
1280.event: Warriors spare the one who blinks and the one who fled, in the manner of heroes.

claims.claim: the heroic way is not to strike with scorn at one who flinches and not to shame one who has fled

links.note: 1259 pitches the camp on Arungalam hill; 1266 sets the two armies against one another.
links.teaches: The poet readies the field in one verse and the clash in the next, so the camp's choice of ground leads straight into the fight.

links.note: 1261 has the eldest brother vow vengeance; 1265 has the lord, cooled by the brothers' words, send them to fight.
links.teaches: The brothers' vow of vengeance is turned into their lord's permission and a goal of making their names stand.

links.note: 1262 has a brother laugh at the humans; 1270 shows the warriors as too great for the world.
links.teaches: The laughing Vidyadharas misjudge their foe, since the poet next shows those warriors as towering figures.

links.note: 1280 has victors decline to strike the blinker or shame the fled; Kural 775 calls a blink at a spear flight.
links.teaches: The epic shows the winners declining to treat a blink as flight, a gentler ending than the couplet's flat verdict.

gains.a: The epic's chivalry is measured against the couplet's strict rule that a blink is already defeat.
gains.b: The couplet's reflex of valour is shown with a winner's answer, mercy to the one who flinches, which it alone never gives.

links.note: 1279 has warriors who do not fear Death send the fearful away; Kural 765 calls an army one that stands against raging Death.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's test of an army into a selection, since warriors themselves dismiss those who fear.

gains.a: The warriors' call gets a standard for whom to keep, since the couplet names fearlessness before Death as what makes an army.
gains.b: The couplet's standing together is given a speaking crowd who sort themselves, which the couplet itself does not show.

links.note: 1256 closes that no one finishes an aim except by hard ripening after kings flee; Kural 473 says many who rose on enthusiasm broke midway.
links.teaches: The epic offers no cause for the kings' failure, while the couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength.

gains.a: The generalising closing lines get a stated cause of ruin, rising without knowing one's strength.
gains.b: The couplet's warning gets a scene of kings who marched and fled, which makes the broken rise concrete.

source_issues: Verses 1274, 1275, 1277 and 1280 had a line repaired for a stray pulli.
Verse 1279 line 1 ends with a corrupt word (ஏற்க்) and its line 2 is metrically irregular.
Many words in 1257 to 1262 are run together, so speakers are held loosely.
